title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the longest substring that can become one repeated uppercase letter with at most k replacements.
Idea: `counts` tracks letters in the current window; `max_freq` records the largest count seen, and `left` advances while window length minus that frequency exceeds k.
Technique and why it applies: A sliding window grows rightward and shrinks when the non-majority characters would require too many replacements.
Invariant: After shrinking, the current window length is the candidate length recorded in `best`, and its frequency counts reflect the active boundaries.
Edge cases: Empty s returns zero; k=0 allows only runs of equal letters; all identical letters need no replacements. Character indexing assumes uppercase A-Z.
Complexity: O(n) time because each boundary moves forward at most n times; O(1) space for 26 counters.
complexity_reason: The right and left pointers each move at most n positions, and `counts` has 26 entries.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the maximum substring length achievable by replacing at most k uppercase characters.
Idea: `cnt` counts letters between `left` and `right`; `maxFreq` tracks the highest seen frequency, and the while condition advances `left` when other letters exceed the replacement budget.
Technique and why it applies: Sliding-window boundaries examine all feasible stretches without restarting for every substring.
Invariant: The counter array represents the current window, and `best` is the longest valid candidate measured during the scan.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; k=0 restricts the answer to a same-letter run; the code assumes characters lie between A and Z. `maxFreq` is not reduced when the window shrinks, a standard safe upper bound for this maximum-length method.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space for 26 counters.
complexity_reason: Both indices only advance across the string, while `cnt` and scalar state use fixed storage.

title: Construct Quad Tree
notes:
Task and constraints: Build a quadtree for a square binary grid, making uniform regions leaves and mixed regions internal nodes.
Idea: `build(r,c,size)` scans the region against its top-left `value`; if uniform it returns a leaf, otherwise it halves `size` and recursively constructs four quadrants.
Technique and why it applies: Divide and conquer partitions a mixed square into smaller squares until every region is uniform.
Invariant: Each returned node represents exactly the grid square described by its row, column, and size arguments.
Edge cases: A uniform grid becomes one leaf; a mixed 2-by-2 grid splits into four single-cell children; the implementation assumes a nonempty square whose side length supports repeated halving.
Complexity: Worst-case O(n² log n) time from rescanning cells at recursive levels; O(n²) nodes/space in the worst case.
complexity_reason: At each level, regions collectively scan O(n²) cells and the recursion may create O(n²) nodes across O(log n) levels.

title: Construct Quad Tree
notes:
Task and constraints: Represent a square binary grid as a quadtree, using leaves for uniform squares and four children for mixed squares.
Idea: `construct` stores `grid` and calls `build`; `build` compares cells with `grid[r][c]`, returns a leaf if `same`, or creates four nodes using half-size quadrants.
Technique and why it applies: Recursive subdivision reduces a nonuniform square into four smaller regions until each region has one value.
Invariant: A `build(r,c,size)` result describes all and only the cells inside that square, with children matching its four quadrants.
Edge cases: Uniform input returns a single leaf; a mixed 2-by-2 grid produces four size-one children; empty grids are not guarded and would fail at `grid.length` or `grid[r][c]`. The side length is assumed compatible with quadtree splitting.
Complexity: Worst-case O(n² log n) time from repeated region scans and O(n²) space for nodes and recursion.
complexity_reason: Each recursive level scans regions totaling O(n²) cells, and a fully mixed grid can produce O(n²) nodes.

title: N-ary Tree Level Order Traversal
notes:
Task and constraints: Return N-ary tree values as lists ordered by depth, from the root level downward.
Idea: `q` begins with root; each loop snapshots the queue length, pops exactly that many nodes into `level`, and appends their children before storing the level in `out`.
Technique and why it applies: Breadth-first search processes nodes FIFO, so a fixed queue-size snapshot isolates one depth at a time.
Invariant: At the start of each outer iteration, `q` contains nodes from one tree depth in left-to-right encounter order.
Edge cases: A null root returns []; a single node returns one one-value level; a node with no children adds no new queue entries. Child order is preserved from each `children` list.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space for the queue and output.
complexity_reason: Each node is enqueued and removed once, and the result stores every node value.

title: N-ary Tree Level Order Traversal
notes:
Task and constraints: Group an N-ary tree's node values by depth, starting with the root and moving downward.
Idea: `levelOrder` returns an empty list for null root, then uses `q.size()` as the current level width, polls that many `Node` objects, and adds their children to the queue.
Technique and why it applies: FIFO breadth-first traversal visits all nodes at depth d before depth d+1, allowing each loop to form one output list.
Invariant: At each outer loop start, the queue contains the unprocessed nodes of the next depth in encounter order.
Edge cases: Null root returns an empty result; a leaf produces a one-element level; null `children` is skipped. `ArrayDeque` cannot store null child references, so the tree structure must not enqueue null nodes.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space for the queue and returned levels.
complexity_reason: Every node enters and leaves `q` once, and all node values are retained in `out`.

title: Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List
notes:
Task and constraints: Flatten a multilevel doubly linked list so each child list follows its parent while next and prev links remain consistent.
Idea: `cur` walks the list; when `cur.child` exists, its former `next` is saved on `stack`, the child becomes next, and child links are repaired. Saved successors are restored when a branch ends.
Technique and why it applies: An explicit stack preserves postponed next nodes while depth-first traversal inserts child lists in place.
Invariant: The visited prefix is flattened, each connected next/prev pair is reciprocal, and `stack` stores original successors awaiting traversal.
Edge cases: Null head returns null; a node with both child and next postpones its next node; a child pointer is cleared after insertion. The input is assumed to have valid doubly linked structure.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(d) stack space for postponed successors, bounded by list nesting/branching.
complexity_reason: Each node is processed once and each saved successor is pushed and popped at most once.

title: Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List
notes:
Task and constraints: Flatten a multilevel doubly linked list in depth-first order, placing child nodes immediately after their parent.
Idea: `cur` follows `next`; when a child exists, the current successor is pushed onto `stack`, the child is connected as `next`, its `prev` is set, and `child` is cleared. At a tail, a saved successor is restored.
Technique and why it applies: Stack-based pointer rewiring defers later siblings while completely traversing a child list first.
Invariant: `cur` traverses the flattened prefix, and each restored successor receives a reciprocal `prev` link from the node before it.
Edge cases: Null head returns null; a child plus a next node requires saving that next node; child pointers are nulled to avoid retaining the multilevel structure. `ArrayDeque` requires non-null pushed nodes.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(d) auxiliary stack space for postponed successors.
complexity_reason: Every node is visited once and each saved `Node` successor is pushed and popped at most once.

title: Minimum Genetic Mutation
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the fewest one-character gene mutations from startGene to endGene using only genes in bank.
Idea: `allowed` is a set of bank genes; BFS stores `(gene,d)` in `q`, tries every A/C/G/T substitution at each position, and uses `seen` to avoid revisiting accepted genes.
Technique and why it applies: Breadth-first search finds the shortest path when each single-character mutation has unit cost.
Invariant: A queued gene's distance is the minimum number of mutations from startGene, and `seen` prevents duplicate queue entries.
Edge cases: Equal start and end returns zero; an endGene absent from bank returns -1; unreachable end returns -1 after the queue empties. The generated endGene is checked before bank membership, but an initial membership guard ensures it is allowed.
Complexity: O(B·L·4·L) time with string construction for B reachable genes of length L; O(B) space for the set and queue.
complexity_reason: Each visited gene tests four replacements at every position and the set and queue store at most B genes.

title: Minimum Genetic Mutation
notes:
Task and constraints: Compute the minimum number of valid single-base changes from startGene to endGene, with intermediate genes restricted to bank.
Idea: `allowed` holds bank strings, `q` starts at startGene, and `d` records each discovered gene's distance. For each position, `a` is mutated through A/C/G/T and restored afterward.
Technique and why it applies: BFS explores gene states in increasing mutation count, so the first generated endGene is reached with minimum steps.
Invariant: Each gene in `d` has its shortest known distance and is enqueued only once; restoring `a[i]` preserves the original character for the next position.
Edge cases: Equal endpoints return zero; a missing endGene returns -1; no route also returns -1. Replacing a character with itself is harmless because `d` suppresses repeats. `new String(a)` allocates candidates during search.
Complexity: O(B·L·4·L) time due to candidate string creation and O(B·L) stored characters across the map/queue.
complexity_reason: The BFS processes each discovered gene once, creates up to four candidate strings per position, and stores visited strings and distances.

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
notes:
Task and constraints: Remove the fewest intervals so the remaining intervals do not overlap.
Idea: `intervals.sort` orders by finish time; `kept` counts intervals whose start is at least the last selected `end`, then the answer subtracts kept from the total.
Technique and why it applies: Earliest-finish-time greedy selection leaves the largest remaining time window for later intervals, maximizing the number retained.
Invariant: `end` is the finish of the last retained interval, and `kept` is the size of a compatible set selected from the processed sorted prefix.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; intervals touching at endpoints are accepted because `start>=end`; identical intervals keep one and count the others for removal. Sorting mutates the input list.
Complexity: O(n log n) time for sorting plus a linear scan; O(1) auxiliary scan space apart from sorting implementation.
complexity_reason: The code sorts n intervals and then inspects each interval once while maintaining `kept` and `end`.

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the minimum removals needed to make all retained intervals non-overlapping.
Idea: `Arrays.sort` orders `intervals` by ending coordinate; the loop increments `kept` when `x[0]>=end` and updates `end` to that interval's finish.
Technique and why it applies: Greedy interval scheduling maximizes retained intervals by always selecting the compatible interval that finishes earliest.
Invariant: After each sorted item, `kept` is the number selected without overlap and `end` is the latest finish among those selected.
Edge cases: An empty array returns zero; touching intervals are compatible under `>=`; duplicates overlap and only one is retained. Sorting changes the input array's order. The long sentinel safely starts below all int endpoints.
Complexity: O(n log n) time for sorting and O(n) for the scan; auxiliary space depends on Java's sort implementation.
complexity_reason: `Arrays.sort` dominates at O(n log n), and the following loop processes each interval once.

title: Path Sum III
notes:
Task and constraints: Count downward binary-tree paths summing to targetSum; each path may start at any node but must follow parent-to-child links.
Idea: `dfs` accumulates `total`, counts prior prefixes equal to `total-targetSum`, increments `prefix[total]`, recurses into children, then decrements that prefix to backtrack.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix sums convert each path-sum check into a lookup for the earlier running total needed to leave targetSum between two prefixes.
Invariant: `prefix` contains counts of prefix sums on the current root-to-node path only, before entering a child.
Edge cases: Null root returns zero; a single node equal to target contributes one; negative node values are supported because the map tracks sums rather than relying on monotonic totals. Backtracking prevents sibling paths from mixing.
Complexity: O(n) expected time and O(h) map/recursion space along a tree path.
complexity_reason: Each node performs a constant number of prefix-map operations and is visited once; active prefixes and recursion follow tree height h.

title: Path Sum III
notes:
Task and constraints: Count downward paths in a binary tree whose values total targetSum, with paths beginning and ending at arbitrary nodes.
Idea: `dfs` adds `n.val` to `sum`, looks up `sum-target`, increments the current prefix count, visits both children, and decrements the count before returning.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix-sum frequencies count how many earlier ancestors create a path with the requested sum, including paths that begin below the root.
Invariant: `prefix` represents running sums on the current recursion path; decrementing on return removes the current node's prefix before exploring a sibling.
Edge cases: Null root contributes zero; a root matching target counts one path; negative values remain valid. `long sum` reduces overflow risk in cumulative totals, though the returned path count is an int.
Complexity: O(n) expected time and O(h) active map entries and recursion stack.
complexity_reason: Each node makes a constant number of HashMap operations and is visited once, with active recursion proportional to height h.

title: Find All Anagrams in a String
notes:
Task and constraints: Return all start indices where a substring of s is an anagram of p, using lowercase letters.
Idea: `need` counts letters in p and `win` tracks a window of length k; each new character increments its count, the character k positions back is removed, and equal arrays trigger an index.
Technique and why it applies: Fixed-size sliding windows compare character-frequency vectors, which are equal exactly when the substring is a permutation of p.
Invariant: Once i reaches k-1, `win` represents exactly the length-k substring ending at i.
Edge cases: If p is longer than s, return []; repeated letters require matching counts, not just membership; when p and s have equal length, only index zero can be returned. Empty p is outside typical constraints and would make the window condition unusual.
Complexity: O(n + |p|) time with 26-entry comparisons per window, effectively O(n) for a fixed alphabet; O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The code counts p once and then slides across s, comparing two fixed 26-element arrays at each full window.

title: Find All Anagrams in a String
notes:
Task and constraints: Find each index where a length-|p| substring of s has exactly p's lowercase-letter frequencies.
Idea: `need` and `win` are 26-entry arrays; the loop adds `s.charAt(i)`, removes the character at `i-k` once the window is too long, and uses `Arrays.equals` to record matching starts.
Technique and why it applies: A fixed-length window maintains letter counts incrementally, so anagram checks compare frequency arrays rather than sorting substrings.
Invariant: For i>=k-1, `win` contains the counts of the current k-character substring ending at i.
Edge cases: p longer than s returns an empty list; repeated letters are handled by counts; an equal-length pair checks only start zero. The code assumes lowercase English letters and positive p length under the usual constraints.
Complexity: O(n + |p|) time for updates plus 26 comparisons per window, and O(1) extra space beyond output.
complexity_reason: The scan updates constant-size arrays and performs a 26-slot equality comparison for each full window.

title: K-th Smallest in Lexicographical Order
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the kth integer in lexicographic order among 1 through n without generating the full sorted list.
Idea: `steps(prefix,next_prefix)` counts numbers under a decimal prefix by summing clipped ranges at each digit depth. The main loop skips a subtree when its count fits k, otherwise descends by multiplying `curr` by ten.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix-tree counting skips whole lexicographic subtrees, avoiding enumeration of every integer before the answer.
Invariant: `curr` is the current prefix in lexicographic traversal, and k is the number of positions still to advance from it.
Edge cases: k=1 returns 1; n=13 follows prefixes 1, 10, 11, 12, 13; when a subtree count equals k it is skipped. Inputs are assumed to satisfy 1<=k<=n.
Complexity: O(log n·log n) time in the straightforward bound for repeated prefix counting and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Each `steps` call walks decimal depths, and the outer traversal advances or descends through at most O(n) prefix positions in its worst-case bound.

title: K-th Smallest in Lexicographical Order
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the kth number in lexicographic order from 1 through n using prefix subtree sizes.
Idea: `curr` starts at 1 and k is decremented to zero-based form; `steps` counts values under `curr`, then the loop either skips that subtree by incrementing curr or descends by multiplying it by ten.
Technique and why it applies: Counting the numbers sharing a decimal prefix allows whole lexicographic ranges to be skipped without sorting all n values.
Invariant: `curr` identifies the current lexicographic node and k counts how many positions remain before the target within the traversal.
Edge cases: k=1 returns 1; for n=13 the order begins 1,10,11,12,13,2; large n needs `long` for `curr`, `first`, `next`, and subtree counts before the final int cast. k is assumed valid.
Complexity: O(log² n) typical prefix-counting time, with O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Each call to `steps` processes decimal digit levels and the main loop uses a constant number of long variables.

title: Arranging Coins
notes:
Task and constraints: Given n coins, find the largest number of complete staircase rows, requiring r(r+1)/2 coins for r rows.
Idea: `lo` and `hi` bound the answer; the upper midpoint is tested against the triangular-number formula, and the search keeps the feasible half.
Technique and why it applies: Binary search finds the greatest row count whose required coin total does not exceed n, exploiting monotonic growth of triangular numbers.
Invariant: The answer remains within [lo,hi], and lo is always a feasible row count.
Edge cases: n=0 returns zero; n=1 returns one; n=5 returns two because three rows require six coins. The upper midpoint avoids stalling when lo and hi differ by one.
Complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) extra space.
complexity_reason: Each iteration halves the inclusive search interval and stores only `lo`, `hi`, and `mid`.

title: Arranging Coins
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the number of full staircase rows buildable from n coins, where r rows use r(r+1)/2 coins.
Idea: `lo` and `hi` are long bounds; the upper midpoint's triangular total is compared with n, and the feasible lower bound or upper bound is adjusted.
Technique and why it applies: Binary search locates the maximum r satisfying the monotone triangular-number inequality.
Invariant: lo is feasible and the answer remains between lo and hi until both bounds meet.
Edge cases: n=0 returns zero; n=1 returns one; n=5 returns two. `long` prevents `mid*(mid+1)` from overflowing int during the comparison, and the final answer fits int for int n.
Complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The search interval shrinks by roughly half per iteration, using a fixed number of long variables.
